query: Consider the following context: High-temperature self-lubricating materials with stable tribological performance across a wide temperature range are essential for advanced mechanical systems under extreme conditions. However, balancing mechanical strength and lubrication efficiency remains a key challenge. In that context, which material can be used for high-performance wide-temperature self-lubricating materials, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a controlled amount of tungsten disulfide (WS2) nanoprecipitates into a tungsten refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) will yield a self‐lubricating material that maintains high mechanical strength and low friction across a wide temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy prepared via methods such as stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations without intentionally incorporated lubricious phases.
generation.intervention: Introduce and control the formation of WS2 nanoprecipitates either during alloy synthesis or via post-processing treatments to enable in situ self-lubricating behavior.
generation.conditions: Performance to be evaluated at ambient, intermediate, and high-temperature conditions (e.g., up to 800°C or above) in inert to moderately oxidizing atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of coherent WS2 nanoprecipitates within the tungsten matrix, which can form a layered, lubricious structure at surfaces while coexisting with the strengthening features of the RHEA.
generation.mechanism: The tungsten matrix maintains ultrahigh strength and ductility via mechanisms such as stepwise coherent nanoprecipitations, while the WS2 phases act as solid lubricants due to their layered crystal structure that facilitates easy shear. This synergy is expected to balance the strength-lubrication trade-off, ensuring low friction and wear over a wide temperature span.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline tungsten refractory alloy, the composite material will have a lower friction coefficient and stable tribological performance without sacrificing its high strength and ductility across a wide temperature range.
generation.baseline: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy produced without lubricious WS2 phases that exhibits high strength but may have suboptimal self-lubricating performance under extreme or variable temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected in environments where oxidation of WS2 is limited; in highly oxidizing conditions at very high temperatures, the WS2 might deteriorate, potentially compromising lubrication.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term stability of the WS2 phases under prolonged high-temperature and reactive environments, as well as the precise balance between strength and lubrication efficiency, needs experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize samples of tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy with and without a controlled addition of WS2 (or conditions that promote in situ WS2 nanoprecipitate formation). Characterize the microstructure (to confirm the presence and coherence of WS2 nanoprecipitates) and perform tribological tests (e.g., friction and wear measurements) as well as mechanical strength tests over a wide temperature range (from room temperature to 800°C or higher). Compare the performance metrics of the modified alloy against the baseline material.
measurements: Friction coefficient measured by pin-on-disk or similar tribometer tests at various temperatures
Wear rate and surface morphology analyses via SEM/AFM
Microstructural characterization via TEM to verify WS2 nanoprecipitate formation and coherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of WS2 nanoprecipitates does not lead to a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient (e.g., 20% lower than baseline) while maintaining mechanical properties comparable to the baseline (within ±10% variation) across the tested temperature range, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] . Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
